title: A dimensionless universal curve collapse: do different cases fall on one curve?
summary: Data from several cases look different in raw units. Rescaled by the right combination of the case parameter they fall on one master curve, which shows the physics depends only on that combination.

media.alt: Left: four saturating curves of different heights and widths for cases A to D. Right: the same data rescaled so all four sets of markers lie on one white universal curve rising from 0 to a plateau at 0.5.
media.caption: Reference render of class F1.8 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: Do different cases collapse onto one curve?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: raw x and y in the case's own units; the plateau height and the rise length both grow with L. Right: x / L^(1/2) on the horizontal axis and y / L on the vertical axis, with a white line for the universal curve.
look_at: On the left, how does the plateau height depend on L? Read it for each case.
On the right, do the four marker sets overlap one curve over the whole range?
Where is the scatter largest and is it systematic or random?
Which marker shape is which case? Shapes, not only colours, name the cases.
as_drawn: Cases A to D have L = 1, 2, 4, 8. Raw plateaus sit at 0.5, 1, 2 and 4: proportional to L.
The scaled panel collapses all four onto y/L = 0.5 tanh^2(0.9 x/L^(1/2)), drawn as a white line. Remaining scatter is a percent or two at the plateau.
Cases differ by marker shape, colour and line style. The scaled panel has no uncertainty bars.
read_the_figure.proves: That, for these cases, the response depends on x and L only through the combinations x / L^(1/2) and y / L. It does not prove that those are the only relevant variables, nor that the same collapse persists outside the tested range of L.
if_wrong: Cases distinguished by colour alone: when the markers overlap, the collapse cannot be audited.
Collapse shown only on log-log axes with a wide scatter: a tight look can hide a 20 percent mismatch.
Exponents of the scaling fitted until the curves overlap and then offered as a discovery: circular.

terms.meaning: A ratio of quantities with the same units, so it carries no unit and is the same in any unit system.
A combination x / L^a of a coordinate with a case parameter chosen so cases coincide.
The single function that all rescaled cases follow.
The overlap of rescaled data onto one curve.
A system with n variables and k basic dimensions can be described by n - k dimensionless groups.
The saturation value the curve approaches.

remember: Collapse means y/L^b is a function of x/L^a only.
Find exponents from raw data: plateau against L, feature position against L, each on log-log.
Mark cases by marker shape as well as colour.
Show the residuals: collapse is a statement to be tested, not eyeballed.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Each marker set is one case, named by colour, marker shape and line style. Position encodes the variable: raw units on the left, scaled units on the right. The white line is the claim being tested: one function for all cases.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: If a response has a characteristic length and size, rescaling by them removes the case parameter. Plotting y/L against x/L^(1/2) makes the four curves identical when y = L Phi(x / L^(1/2)). The left panel shows what the eye misses (the pattern is hidden by different scales); the right panel shows the structure. A collapse is evidence that you identified the right dimensionless groups.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Collapse can be forced: choosing exponents to make curves overlap proves nothing alone. A log axis can hide a large mismatch. A short x range or few cases makes agreement easy. And a collapse onto a curve says nothing about quantities that were not rescaled, such as an extra variable you did not vary.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: Marker shapes allow a reader (and a colour-blind reader) to see whether one case is the outlier. The raw panel next to the scaled panel shows that the collapse is real work, not a trick of presentation.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Plot the difference between each case and the master curve against the scaled x, on a linear axis. Put the exponents' fitted values with uncertainties in the legend. Use Buckingham pi to predict the groups before looking at the data.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a lower panel with residuals (y/L minus the master curve) for each case, with a band of plus and minus the measurement uncertainty.

steps.title: What collapse means
steps.note: With Y and X as the plot coordinates the case parameter L has disappeared from the relation: every case lies on the same Phi.

steps.title: Reading the exponents from raw data
steps.tex: y_\mathrm{plateau}\propto L^{a}\ \text{and}\ x_{1/2}\propto L^{b}:\quad a=\frac{\Delta\log y_\mathrm{plateau}}{\Delta\log L},\ b=\frac{\Delta\log x_{1/2}}{\Delta\log L}
steps.note: For this data a = 1 (plateau 0.5, 1, 2, 4 for L = 1, 2, 4, 8) and b = 1/2 (the half-plateau point sits at x = 0.98 sqrt L: 0.98, 1.38, 1.96, 2.77).

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) what are the raw plateau heights and how do they depend on L? (2) Where do the cases reach half their plateau after scaling? (3) Is the collapse good everywhere?

solution.text: Plateaus at 0.5, 1, 2, 4 for L = 1, 2, 4, 8: proportional to L, so the right scaling for y is y / L.
After scaling, all cases reach half of the 0.5 plateau at X about 0.98.
The markers lie on the curve everywhere; only the plateau shows a percent or two of scatter.

worked.answer: y scales with L, x with sqrt(L); a single function describes all cases, with about 1 to 2 percent scatter at the plateau.

analyze.q: The best-fit exponents are 1 and 0.5. Suppose a case with L = 16 does not collapse. Give two possible reasons.
analyze.hint: Another variable changed, or the physics leaves the regime.

analyze.q: Why show the raw panel next to the scaled one?
analyze.hint: What does the reader learn about the effort of the scaling?

analyze.q: How would you test the collapse numerically instead of by eye?

evaluate.q: A collapse on log-log axes looks perfect with exponent 0.5, but a fit on linear axes says 0.45. Which do you trust and why?

create: Take the Taylor blast-wave idea R proportional to (E t^2 / rho)^(1/5) and plot data from several energies as R / (E / rho)^(1/5) against t^(2/5).
Plot residuals of the collapse for each case.

checks.q: What does it mean when different cases lie on a single curve after rescaling?
checks.hint: Think of what variables the curve depends on.
checks.answer: The response depends on x and the case parameter only through the scaled combination, so a single function describes all cases.

checks.q: Plateaus are 0.5, 1, 2, 4 for L = 1, 2, 4, 8. Which power of L scales y?
checks.answer: y / L: the plateau divided by L is 0.5 for every case.

checks.q: A collapse looks perfect on a log-log plot. Why should you still plot the residuals on a linear axis?
checks.answer: A log-log plot turns a 20 percent difference into a small gap. Residuals on linear axes show whether the mismatch is systematic.
